parts.label: (a)(i)

markscheme_points.text: emission of electrons (from a metal surface)
when electromagnetic radiation is incident (on electrons)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what shines onto the metal and what particle comes out of the metal surface as a result.
Hint 2: State the definition clearly: the emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation is incident on it.
parts.proper_answer: Emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation is incident on the surface.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Happens At The Surface**
Imagine shining light onto a clean metal plate in a vacuum. You are putting light in, and something material comes out that can be detected as a current. That something is electrons leaving the metal.

Step 2: **Build The Precise Definition**
So the photoelectric effect is the release of electrons from a metal surface caused by incident electromagnetic radiation such as visible light or ultraviolet. The key words are emission, electrons, metal surface, and incident radiation.

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: minimum energy required for an electron to leave

hints: Hint 1: Think of an electron trapped inside the metal - what is the smallest amount of energy it must gain to just get free with no spare kinetic energy?
parts.proper_answer: Minimum energy required for an electron to escape from the metal surface.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why An Electron Needs Help To Leave**
Electrons in a metal are attracted to the positive ions. To leave completely they must do work against that attraction.

Step 2: **Minimum Means Just Free**
The work function energy $\Phi$ is that minimum energy bill. If the electron gets exactly $\Phi$ it just escapes with zero kinetic energy. Any more energy becomes kinetic energy outside the metal.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A polished calcium plate in a vacuum is investigated by illuminating the surface with light.

It is found that no photoelectric current is produced when the frequency of the light is less than $6.93 \times 10^{14}\text{Hz}$.
parts.text: State the name of the frequency below which no photoelectric current is produced.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the special name given to the minimum light frequency that can still just release electrons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Frequency To No Current**
You are told that below $6.93 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ no electrons come out at all, so no photoelectric current. That cut-off value has its own name.

Step 2: **Name The Cut-Off**
It is called the threshold frequency $f_0$. Light of frequency $f < f_0$ can never cause emission, however intense or long it shines.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how the photon model of electromagnetic radiation accounts for this phenomenon.

markscheme_points.text: • photons are (discrete) packets of energy • energy of photons depends on frequency (of EM radiation) • electrons can only absorb a single photon (of energy) (Any two points, 1 mark each)
emission only possible if photon energy is at least the work function

hints: Hint 1: In the photon model, electromagnetic radiation consists of discrete packets of energy (photons), where each photon carries energy $E = hf$.
Hint 2: Each electron at the metal surface interacts with and absorbs only one single photon at a time.
Hint 3: To escape, an electron must absorb at least the work function energy $\Phi$; if $hf < \Phi$, no emission can occur regardless of intensity, defining a threshold frequency.
parts.proper_answer: Light consists of discrete packets of energy called photons with energy $hf$. An electron absorbs a single photon in a one-to-one interaction. Emission occurs only if $hf$ is at least equal to the work function, so below the threshold frequency no emission is possible.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Light As Packets**
In the photon model, electromagnetic radiation travels as discrete packets of energy called photons. Each photon carries energy: $$E = hf$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant and $f$ is the frequency. Higher frequency means a more energetic photon.

Step 2: **One Photon Per Electron**
An electron at the surface can absorb only one photon at a time in a single interaction. It cannot save up energy from many dim photons. So its available energy is just the energy of that one photon.

Step 3: **Why A Cut-Off Exists**
To escape, the electron needs at least the work function $\Phi$. So we need: $$hf \ge \Phi$$ If $f$ is too low, $hf < \Phi$ and even absorbing a whole photon is not enough. Increasing intensity only gives more photons, not more energetic photons, so no current appears below $f_0$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the work function energy, in $\text{eV}$, of calcium.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the threshold condition where the photon just provides the minimum escape energy, using the given $f_0 = 6.93 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.
Hint 2: Calculate $\Phi = hf_0$ in joules with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$, then divide by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ to convert to $\text{eV}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use The Threshold Condition**
At the threshold frequency the photon energy exactly equals the work function, with zero excess kinetic energy: $$\Phi = hf_0$$ You know $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $f_0 = 6.93 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.

Step 2: **Calculate In Joules Then Convert To eV**
First in joules: $$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(6.93 \times 10^{14}) = 4.59 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$ Then convert using $1 \text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$: $$\Phi = \frac{4.59 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.87 \text{ eV}$$ This small eV value is typical for a metal work function.
